title: Of the affection of fathers to their children
paragraphs: To Madame d'Estissac.

Madam, if the strangeness and novelty of my subject — which usually give things their value — do not save me, I shall never come out of this foolish attempt with any honour: but the subject is so fantastic, and so unlike anything in common usage, that this, perhaps, may carry it off. It was a melancholy mood, and consequently a mood very contrary to my natural complexion, brought on by the brooding solitude into which I have for some years now retired, that first put into my head this idle fancy of writing. Finding myself totally unprovided with any other matter, I offered myself to myself as subject and argument. It is the only book in the world of its kind, and a wild and extravagant project. Nothing about the business is worth notice except that extravagance; for in a subject so empty and frivolous, even the best workman in the world could not have given it a shape fit to recommend it for any kind of esteem.

Now, madam, having to draw my own portrait to the life, I would have left out an important feature if I had not also represented the honour I have always had for you and your merits — which I have deliberately chosen to put at the start of this chapter, because, among the many other fine qualities you possess, the tender love you have shown your children stands very high. Whoever knows at what age Monsieur d'Estissac, your husband, left you a widow; the great and honourable matches that have since been offered to you, as many as to any lady of your rank in France; the constancy and steadiness with which, for so many years, you have borne so many sharp difficulties, the burden and conduct of business that has hounded you in every corner of the kingdom, and is not yet tired of harassing you; and the happy result you have given to all of it, by your own prudence or good fortune — anyone who knows all that will easily agree with me that we have no more vivid example of maternal devotion in our times than yours. I thank God, madam, that it has been so well placed; for the great hopes that Monsieur d'Estissac your son gives of himself are firm enough that when he comes of age you will harvest from him all the obedience and gratitude of a very good man. But since, on account of his tender years, he has not been able to take in those services of the highest value which he has received from you in such number, I want, if these papers should one day come into his hands when I no longer have mouth or speech to tell him myself, that he should receive from me a true account of what is being more effectively shown to him by its effects already: namely, that there is no gentleman in France more indebted to a mother's care, and that he cannot, in the future, give better or more certain proof of his own worth and virtue than by acknowledging you for the excellent mother that you are.

If there is any law that is truly natural — that is to say, any instinct that can be seen universally and permanently imprinted in both animals and men (which is open to dispute) — I would say that, in my opinion, next to each creature's care for its own preservation and avoidance of what may hurt it, the affection which the begetter bears towards his offspring holds second place. And since nature seems to have entrusted it to us, in view of the extension and continuation of the successive pieces of her machinery, it is no wonder if, on the other side, that of children towards their parents is not as great. Add to this the Aristotelian observation that whoever does a benefit to someone loves him more than he is loved back by him; that the giver loves more than the receiver; and that every craftsman is fonder of his work than the work, if it had feeling, would be of him — since it is dear to us to be, and to be consists in motion and activity, so that every man has in some sort a being in his work. A benefactor performs a fine and honourable action; the one who receives the benefit performs only a useful action. Now the useful is far less loveable than the honourable; the honourable is stable and lasting, giving the man who has done it a continuing satisfaction. The useful slips away easily and the memory of it is neither so fresh nor so pleasant. The things dearest to us are those that have cost us most, and giving is more costly than receiving.

Since it has pleased God to give us some capacity for reason, in order that we should not, like the animals, be slavishly subject to the laws common to both, but should accept them by judgement and willing freedom, we ought, indeed, to give something to the simple authority of nature, but not let ourselves be tyrannically swept along by her; reason alone should guide our inclinations. For my part, I have an odd distaste for those impulses that are set off in us without the mediation and direction of judgement. On the subject I am dealing with, I cannot share that passion for dandling and caressing infants barely born, with neither motion of soul nor shape of body distinguishable enough to make them lovable, and I have not willingly let them be nursed near me. A true and well-regulated affection ought to be born and to grow along with our knowledge of what they are; then, if they prove worthy of it, natural inclination walking hand in hand with reason, we should cherish them with a truly fatherly love — and likewise, if they are not, we should still defer to reason in spite of the pull of nature. Most of the time it works the other way round. Usually we are more taken with the running about, the games, and the childish silliness of our children than we are, later, with their most accomplished doings — as if we had loved them as our playthings, like monkeys, and not as men; and there are some who will spend liberally to buy them toys to play with, but become very tight-fisted about the slightest necessary expense once they grow up. In fact, it looks as if jealousy at seeing them appear in and enjoy the world just as we are about to leave it makes us stingier and meaner towards them; it vexes us that they are treading on our heels, as if pushing us out. If that were really something to be feared — since the order of things is such that, to tell the truth, they cannot exist or live except at the expense of our being and life — then we ought never to have become fathers at all.

For my part, I think it cruelty and injustice not to admit them to a share of our goods and to fellowship in our domestic affairs once they are capable of it, and not to cut down our own spending to make more room for theirs, since this is what we begot them for. It is unjust that an old fellow, broken and half-dead, should alone in his chimney corner enjoy the money that would be enough to maintain and advance several children, leaving them, meanwhile, to lose their best years for want of means to make their way in public service and in the knowledge of the world. A man, by doing this, drives them to despair, and to seek out, by whatever means however dishonest, a way of supporting themselves. I have seen in my time several young men of good family so given to stealing that no correction could cure them. I knew one of a very good family to whom, at the request of a brother of his — a very honest and brave gentleman — I once spoke about this, and he answered, candidly admitting to me, that he had been driven into this shabby practice by the severity and greed of his father, but that he was now so used to it that he could not stop. And at that very time he had been caught stealing a lady's rings, having gone into her room when she was dressing along with several others. He reminded me of a story I had heard about another gentleman, so thoroughly trained in this fine trade in his youth that, after coming into his estate and resolving to give it up, he still could not keep his hands off anything he saw he liked in a shop as he passed by, even though he had to bear the shame of sending afterwards to pay for it. And I have myself seen several so habituated to this quality that even among their own friends they could not stop themselves from filching, though they meant to return what they had taken. I am a Gascon, and yet there is no vice I understand less than this one; I hate it more from temperament than I condemn it by reason. I do not even covet anything that belongs to someone else. This province of ours, in plain truth, has a rather worse reputation in this respect than the other parts of the kingdom; and yet several times in our own day we have seen men of good families from other provinces brought before the courts and convicted of abominable thefts. I am afraid this vice is, in some way, to be blamed on the same vice of the fathers I have been talking about.

And if anyone should tell me, as a very intelligent lord once did, that "he was hoarding wealth not to get any other use out of his thrift but to make himself respected and sought after by his relatives; and that, since age had robbed him of all other power, this was his only remaining means of keeping authority in the family and not being neglected and despised by all around him" — in truth, not only old age, but, according to Aristotle, every kind of weakness encourages greed; that is something, but it is medicine for a disease that a man ought to prevent the birth of. A father is very miserable who has no other hold on his children's affection than their need for his help — if that can be called affection. He must make himself worthy of respect by his virtue and wisdom, and worthy of love by his kindness and the sweetness of his manners. Even the ashes of a rich subject have their value; we treat the bones and relics of worthy men with respect and reverence. No old age can be so decrepit, in a man who has lived honourably, that it is not still venerable, especially to his children, whose souls he should have trained to their duty by reason, not by need and dependence on him, nor by harshness and compulsion:
"Et errat longe mea quidem sententia Qui imperium credat esse gravius, aut stabilius, Vi quod fit, quam illud, quod amicitia adjungitur."
["He is much mistaken, in my opinion, who thinks that government more weighty and lasting which rests on force, than that which is held together by friendship." — Terence, Adelphoe, i. 1, 40.]

I condemn all violence in the upbringing of a tender soul designed for honour and freedom. There is something servile about rigour and constraint, and I hold that what cannot be done by reason, prudence, and tact will never be done by force. I myself was raised that way; they tell me that in all my early years I felt the rod only twice, and then very lightly. I have used the same method with my own children, all of whom died at nurse except Léonore, my only daughter, who reached the age of five and more with no other correction for her childish faults (her mother's indulgence readily seconding mine) than words, and very gentle ones at that. Even if my hopes were entirely disappointed in this method, there would be plenty of other causes to lay the fault on without blaming my discipline, which I know to be natural and just; and I would have been still more scrupulous on this point with sons, as less born to subjection and more free, and I would have made it my business to fill their hearts with openness and freedom. I have never observed any other effects of whipping than to make boys either more cowardly or more wilfully stubborn.
Do we wish to be loved by our children? Do we want to remove from them every occasion for wishing our death — though no occasion for so horrible a wish could ever be just or excusable?
"Nullum scelus rationem habet."
["No wickedness has any reason behind it." — Livy, xxviii. 28]

Let us reasonably accommodate their lives with what is in our power. To do this, we should not marry so young that our age is practically confused with theirs; for this disadvantage plunges us into many very great difficulties, especially among the gentry, who are in a station with little to do and live on their rents alone. Elsewhere, among people who live by their work, the multitude and company of children is an addition to the common stock; they are so many new tools and instruments to grow rich with.

I married at thirty-three, and I agree with the opinion fixing the right age at thirty-five, which is said to be Aristotle's. Plato would have nobody marry before thirty, but he has reason to laugh at those who took up marriage after fifty-five, and condemns their offspring as unworthy of food and life. Thales gave the truest limits: when, as a young man, his mother kept urging him to marry, he answered, "It is too soon," and, when he was getting on in years and pressed again, "It is too late." A man must deny opportunity to every inopportune action. The ancient Gauls held it a horrible thing for a man to keep company with a woman before he was twenty, and strongly recommended to men intending themselves for war that they keep their virginity well into their grown years, since courage is sapped and diverted by intercourse with women:
"Ma, or congiunto a giovinetta sposa, E lieto omai de' figli, era invilito Negli affetti di padre et di marito."
["But now, married to a young wife and happy in his children, he had been weakened by the feelings of father and husband." — Tasso, Gerusalemme Liberata, x. 39.]

Muley Hassan, king of Tunis, the one whom the Emperor Charles V restored to his kingdom, reproached the memory of his father Mahomet with his frequenting of women, calling him loose, effeminate, and a begetter of children. The Greek histories tell us that Iccus the Tarentine, Chryso, Astyllus, Diopompos, and others, to keep their bodies in shape for the Olympic games and similar exercises, denied themselves during that training all dealings with Venus. In a certain country of the Spanish Indies men were not allowed to marry until after forty, yet the girls were given over at ten. It is not time for a gentleman of thirty to give place to his son of twenty; he is himself in a position to serve both in war and in the court of his prince; he needs all his resources; and yet, no doubt, he ought to surrender a share — but not so great a share as to forget himself for others. For such a man, the answer fathers usually have at the ready — "I will not take off my clothes before I go to bed" — serves well enough.

But a father worn out by age and infirmities, and cut off by weakness and ill health from the common society of men, wrongs both himself and his family by piling up a great heap of treasure. He has lived long enough, if he is wise, to be willing to undress for bed — not down to the shirt, I admit, but down to it and a good warm dressing-gown; the rest of the pomps, of which he has no further use, he should voluntarily hand over to those to whom, in the order of nature, they belong. It is only reasonable that he should let them have the use of those things, since nature has put him in a state in which he can no longer enjoy them himself; otherwise there is plainly malice and envy in the business. The greatest action of the Emperor Charles V was this: in imitation of some of the ancients of his own rank, recognising that it is reasonable to strip ourselves when our clothes are loading us down and grown too heavy, and to lie down when our legs begin to give way, he resigned his possessions, his greatness, and his power to his son, when he found his vigour and steadiness for the conduct of affairs were failing in a way unworthy of the glory he had won in them:
"Solve senescentem mature sanus equum, ne Peccet ad extremum ridendus, et ilia ducat."
["Dismiss the ageing horse in good time, while you are still sound, lest he stumble in the lists at the end, panting, and the spectators laugh." — Horace, Epistles, i. 1, 8.]

This fault — of not noticing in good time and not feeling the weakness and great alteration that age naturally brings on both body and mind (which, in my opinion, are equal, if indeed the soul does not get more than half) — has cost most of the great men in the world their reputation. I have known in my time, and been on familiar terms with, people of great authority whom one could plainly see had slipped marvellously below the level of competence I knew they once had, judging by the reputation they had built up in their earlier years; I could heartily, for their own sakes, have wished them at home and at ease, freed of public or military positions that had grown too heavy for their shoulders. I was once on very familiar terms in a gentleman's house, the master a widower and very old, though healthy and cheerful enough. He had several daughters to marry off and a son already grown, which brought him a great many visitors and a great deal of expense, neither of which pleased him — not only out of frugality but still more because, on account of his age, he had moved into a way of life very different from ours. I told him one day a little boldly, as I was used to doing, that he would do better to give us younger folk room, and to leave his principal house (for it was his only well-placed and well-furnished one) to his son, while he himself retired to an estate he had nearby, where nobody would disturb his peace; since otherwise he could not avoid being pestered by us, given the situation of his children. He took my advice afterwards, and found himself better off for it.

I do not mean that a man should install them so firmly as to leave himself no liberty of going back on it; I, who have now reached the age when such things are appropriate, would hand over to my children the use of my house and goods, but with the power to take it back if they should give me cause to change my mind; I would leave them the use, that being no longer convenient for me; and of the general authority and power over everything, I would keep back as much as I thought best. I have always held that it must be a great satisfaction to an elderly father to put his children into the way of running his affairs, and to have the power, during his own life, to keep an eye on how they behave, supplying them with instruction and advice from his own experience, and himself to transfer the ancient honour and order of his house into the hands of those who are to come after him, satisfying himself in this way as to the hopes he may entertain of their future conduct. And to do that, I would not avoid their company; I would observe them at close quarters, and share, according to my time of life, in their feasts and gaieties. If I did not live altogether with them — which I could not do without bothering them and their friends, given my age's bad temper and the restlessness of my ailments, and without breaking the rules and order of living I would by then have laid down for myself — I would, at least, live near them in some retired part of my house, not the showiest but the most convenient. And not as I saw, a few years back, a dean of Saint-Hilaire in Poitiers, given over to such a solitude that, at the time I came into his room, it had been twenty-two years since he had set foot outside it, and yet he still had all his movements free and easy, and was in good health except for a cold that had settled on his lungs. He would hardly let anyone in to see him even once a week; he kept himself shut in his room alone, except for a servant who brought him something to eat once a day, and would only come in and go out again. His occupation was to walk up and down and read some book, since he was a bit of a scholar; but as to the rest, he was obstinately set on dying in this retreat, which he soon did. I would try, by pleasant conversation, to build up in my children a warm and unfeigned friendship and goodwill towards me, which is not hard to do with well-born natures; for if they are wild brutes, of which our age produces thousands, then we have only to hate and shun them as such.

I am annoyed at the custom of forbidding children to call their father by the name of father, and making them use some other, supposedly more full of respect and reverence — as if nature had not provided enough authority for us. We call Almighty God Father, and disdain to have our children call us so; I have corrected this mistake in my family. It is also folly and injustice to deprive grown children of familiarity with their father, and to wear a stern and forbidding face in front of them, thinking by that to keep them in awe and obedience; this is a very idle farce that, instead of producing the intended effect, makes fathers obnoxious and, worse still, ridiculous to their own children. The children have youth and vigour in their possession, and consequently the breath and favour of the world; and so they meet these fierce and tyrannical looks — mere scarecrows — of a man with no blood in his heart or veins, with mockery and contempt. Though I could make myself feared, I would much rather make myself loved: there are so many kinds of defects in old age, so much weakness, and it is so open to contempt, that the best gain a man can make is the kindness and affection of his own family; command and fear are no longer his weapons. I knew one who, having been very imperious in his youth, when he grew old, though he could have lived in perfect ease, would always be hitting, shouting, swearing, and cursing — the most violent householder in France — wearing himself out with needless suspicion and vigilance. And all this commotion and uproar only led to his being cheated all the more by his household: of his barn, his kitchen, his cellar — yes, and his very purse too — others had the biggest use and share, while he kept his keys in his pocket more carefully than his eyes. While he congratulated himself on the pitiful frugality of a miserly table, everything was going to wrack and ruin in every corner of his house, in gambling, drinking, every kind of waste, while they made sport in their parties of his pointless anger and useless thrift. Everyone was a sentry against him, and if by chance any poor fellow in his service had a different temper and would not join the rest, the man was at once made suspect to him — a bait old age very easily bites at all on its own. How often had this gentleman boasted to me of how much he kept his family in awe, and how exact an obedience and reverence they paid him, and how clearly he saw into his own affairs!
"Ille solus nescit omnia."
["He alone is ignorant of all that is going on." — Terence, Adelphoe, iv. 2, 9.]

I do not know anyone better equipped, both naturally and by training, to maintain authority than he was; and yet he has fallen from it like a child. For this reason I have picked him out, among several others I know of the same temper, as the strongest example. It would make a question for the schools whether he is better off this way or the other. In his presence, everyone submits to him and bows to him, and humours his vanity to the point where nobody ever contradicts him; he gets his fill of agreement, of feigned fear, submission, and respect. Does he dismiss a servant? The man packs his bundle and is off; but only just out of his sight: old age moves so slowly, the senses are so dulled, that the servant will go on living and doing his old job in the same house for a year without being noticed.

And after a suitable interval, letters are pretended to come from far away, very humble, very apologetic, full of promises of amendment, by which the man is taken back into favour. Does Monsieur make a contract, or order a dispatch which they do not like? It is suppressed, and reasons are then invented to excuse the failure to carry out the one or to answer the other. Since no letters are brought to him first, he sees only those that look fit for his knowledge. If by chance they do fall into his own hand first, since he is used to having someone else read them to him, that reader reads on the fly whatever he sees fit, and often makes someone humbly beg his pardon while in the actual letter he is abusing and reviling the master. In short, he sees nothing except through an image prepared and arranged beforehand, the most flattering they can come up with, so as not to provoke his bad temper and anger. I have seen, in various forms, plenty of these arrangements of household government — long-lasting, steady, all to the same effect.

Women are eternally given to crossing their husbands: they jump at any chance to contradict and oppose them; the slightest pretext serves them as full justification. I knew one who robbed her husband on a large scale so that, as she told her confessor, she could give more generously in alms. Let anyone trust to that pious cover who likes. No conduct of business seems dignified enough to them if it comes from the husband's consent; they must usurp it either by insolence or by cunning, and always at his expense, or else it lacks the grace and authority they want it to have. When, as in the case I am speaking of, it is against a poor old man and on behalf of the children, they take advantage of this title to dress up their passion in glory; and, as in a common cause, they easily plot and gang up against his rule and dominion. If they are sons grown up in full flourishing health, they soon corrupt — by force or favour — the steward, the receivers, and the rest of the household. Men who have neither wife nor son fall into this misfortune less easily, but more cruelly and unworthily when they do. Cato the Elder said in his time, So many servants, so many enemies; consider, then, whether, given the vast difference between the purity of the age he lived in and the corruption of ours, he does not seem to be telling us that wife, son, and servant are all so many enemies to us. It is well for old age that it is always accompanied by lack of observation, ignorance, and a readiness to be deceived. If we did see how we are being treated, and refused to put up with it, what would become of us? — especially in an age such as ours, where the very judges who are supposed to settle our disputes are usually partisans of the young and have an interest in the case. In case the discovery of this cheating escapes me, at least I cannot fail to see that I am thoroughly fit to be cheated. And can anyone ever overpraise the value of a friend, compared with these civil ties? The very image of friendship that I see in animals, so pure and uncorrupted, how reverently I respect it! If others deceive me, at least I do not deceive myself by thinking I can defend myself from them, or by racking my brains to make myself able to. I shield myself from such betrayals within my own breast, not by an anxious and tumultuous curiosity, but rather by diverting my mind and by resolution. When I hear talk of someone's situation, I do not bother to think about him; I turn my eyes at once upon myself, to see what condition I am in; whatever concerns another is also relevant to me. What has happened to him is a warning to me, and rouses me to turn my defence in that direction. We say every day and every hour about other people things we could properly say about ourselves, if only we could apply our observation to our own business as well as we extend it to theirs. Several authors have, in this way, undermined their own case by rushing headlong against those they were attacking, and have flung shafts at their enemies that could more justly, and to greater effect, have been turned against themselves.

The late Marshal de Monluc, having lost his son, who died on the island of Madeira — in truth a very worthy gentleman, of great promise — among his other regrets, dwelt especially on his sorrow and heartbreak that he had never let himself be familiar with him. Out of that habit of paternal gravity and stern looks he had lost the chance of getting to know his son and of letting his son know the extreme affection he had for him in his heart and the worthy opinion he had of his virtue. "That poor boy," he said, "never saw in me anything but a stern and disdainful face, and has gone in the belief that I neither knew how to love him nor to esteem him according to his deserts. For whom was I keeping the disclosure of the singular affection I bore him in my soul? Wasn't it for him himself, who should have had all the pleasure of it and all the gratitude? I constrained and racked myself to put on and keep up that empty disguise, and by doing so I have robbed myself of the pleasure of his company, and, I fear, in some measure of his affection — which could only have been very cold towards me, since I never showed him anything but harshness, and he never felt anything but a tyrannical manner of behaviour from me."
[Madame de Sévigné says that she never read this passage without tears in her eyes. "My God!" she exclaims, "how full this book is of good sense!" — Ed.]

I find this lament reasonable and rightly felt: for as I myself know from too sure an experience, there is no sweeter consolation in the loss of friends than the awareness of having had no reserve or secret from them, and of having had perfect and complete openness with them. Oh my friend, am I better off for feeling this — or worse? I am, without doubt, much the better. I am consoled and honoured in the sorrow for his death. Is it not a holy and gracious office of my life to be always at my friend's funeral? Can there be any joy equal to this loss?

I open myself to my family as much as I can, and very willingly let them know the state of my opinion and goodwill towards them, as I do for everyone else: I hurry to bring myself out and present myself to them; for I do not want them to be mistaken in me on any point. Among other special customs of our ancient Gauls, this was one, as Caesar reports: that sons never came into their fathers' presence, nor dared to appear in their company in public, before they began to bear arms, as if to mean that it was time then for their fathers to admit them into their familiarity and acquaintance.

I have observed yet another kind of bad judgement in fathers of my time, that, not content with having deprived their children, during their own long lives, of the share they should naturally have had in their fortunes, they then leave the same authority over their estates to their wives, and the freedom to dispose of them as they please. I knew one lord — one of the principal officers of the crown — who, with more than fifty thousand crowns yearly income to come to him, died destitute and crushed by debt at over fifty years of age, while his mother in her extreme decrepitude was still in possession of all his property by the will of his father, who himself had lived to nearly eighty. This seems to me anything but reasonable. I therefore think it does a man whose own affairs are in good shape very little good to look for a wife who burdens his estate with a great fortune; there is no kind of debt brought in from outside which brings more ruin to families than that. My predecessors have always been alive to that danger and provided against it, and so have I. But those who advise us against rich wives, for fear they may be less tractable and kind, are mistaken in making a man lose a real advantage for so flimsy a guess. It costs an unreasonable woman no more to go against one reason than another; they cherish themselves most where they are most in the wrong. Injustice attracts them, just as honour from virtuous actions attracts the good; and the more wealth they bring with them, the more good-natured they are, just as beautiful women are all the more inclined and proud to be chaste.

It is reasonable to leave the management of business to the mothers until the children are old enough, according to law, to handle it themselves; but the father has brought them up very badly if he cannot hope that, once they reach maturity, they will have more wisdom and ability in managing affairs than his wife, given the ordinary weakness of the sex. It would, even so, be more against nature, to be truthful, to make the mothers depend on the discretion of their children. They ought to be plentifully provided for, so as to maintain themselves according to their rank and age, since necessity and want are far more unbecoming and unbearable to them than to men; the son should rather be cut short than the mother.

In general, the wisest distribution of our goods, when we come to die, is, in my opinion, to let them be distributed according to the custom of the country; the laws have thought the matter through better than we know how to, and it is wiser to let them fail in their settlement than rashly to run the risk of going wrong in ours. Nor are our goods strictly ours; by civil prescription, even without us, they are all destined for certain heirs. And although we have some liberty beyond that, I think we ought not, without great and obvious cause, to take from anyone what his fortune has assigned him, and to which public equity gives him title; and that it is contrary to reason to abuse this liberty by making it serve our own frivolous and personal whims. My destiny has been kind to me in not putting in my way occasions to tempt me and turn my affection away from the common and lawful course. There are many people for whom it is wasted time to keep up a long course of good services: a word taken amiss wipes out ten years of merit; happy is he who is in a position to grease their goodwill at this last passage. The last action carries it — not the best and most frequent services, but the most recent and present ones do the work. These are people who play with their wills as with apples or rods, to favour or punish every move made by those who lay claim to their care. It is a thing of too much weight and consequence to be tumbled and tossed and altered every moment, and one in which the wise resolve once for all, looking above all to reason and to public custom. We take these male succession arrangements too much to heart, proposing a ridiculous eternity for our names. We are also too superstitious in vain guesses about the future, which we draw from the words and acts of our children. Perhaps people might have done me an injustice in passing me over, since I was the dullest and heaviest, the slowest and most reluctant at my book, not just among my brothers, but among all the boys in the whole province — whether at learning my lesson or at any physical exercise. It is folly to make a choice outside the ordinary order on the credit of these divinations, where we are so often deceived. If the usual rule of descent had to be set aside, and the fates corrected in the choice they had made of our heirs, it could be done more plausibly on account of some striking and serious personal deformity — a permanent and incorrigible defect — and, in the opinion of us French, who are great admirers of beauty, an important drawback.

The pleasant dialogue between Plato's legislator and his citizens will be an ornament to this place. "What," they say, feeling themselves about to die, "are we not free to dispose of what is ours to whomever we please? Good God! What cruelty that it should not be lawful for us, according as we have been served and looked after in our illness, in our old age, in our affairs, to give more or less to those we have found most attentive about us, at our own fancy and discretion!" To which the legislator answers:

"My friends, who are now, without question, very soon to die, it is hard for you in the state you are in either to know yourselves or to know what is yours, as the Delphic inscription puts it. I, who make the laws, am of the opinion that you yourselves are not your own, nor is what is in your hands. Both your goods and you belong to your families, those past and those to come; but, more than that, both your family and your goods belong far more to the public. So, lest some flatterer in your old age or your sickness, or some passion of your own, sway you at a bad moment into making an unjust will, I will take care to prevent that drawback. Looking to both the general interests of the city and the particular one of your family, I will establish laws, and show by sound reasons that private convenience must give way to the common good. Go then cheerfully where human necessity calls you. It is for me — who regard the one no more than the other, and who, as far as I am able, am provident for the public interest — to take care of what you leave behind."

To get back to my subject: it seems to me that women are very rarely born with any natural claim to power over men, apart from the maternal and natural one, unless it is for the punishment of those who, in some amorous fever, have voluntarily put themselves into their hands. But that has nothing to do with the old ones I am speaking of now. This is the consideration that has made us so willing to pass and give force to that law, which has been seen in no other place, by which women are excluded from succession to our crown; and there is hardly a government in the world where it could not be pleaded, as it is here, on the basis of the probability of the reason that supports it — though fortune has given it more credit in some places than in others. It is dangerous to leave the disposal of our succession to their judgement, according to the choice they make among the children, which is often fanciful and unjust; for the irregular cravings and depraved tastes they have during pregnancy stay with them in their minds at other times. We commonly see them fond of the weakest, most rickety, and most deformed children, or of the one — if they have one — still hanging at the breast. For, not having enough force of reason to choose and embrace what is most worthy, they more willingly let themselves be carried away where the impressions of nature are most simply at work, like animals that know their young no longer than they suckle them. As for the rest, it is easy to make out by experience that this natural affection, to which we give such great weight, has very weak roots indeed. For a very small profit, every day we tear their own children out of mothers' arms, and make them take ours in their place; we make them hand over their own to some pitiful nurse, to whom we would not dream of entrusting our own, or to some she-goat, forbidding them not only to give the children suck — whatever danger they may incur by it — but also to take any kind of care of them, so that they may be wholly occupied with the care of and attention to ours. And we see in most of these nurses an adopted affection, more violent than the natural one, springing up by habit towards the foster children, and a greater concern for the preservation of those they have taken charge of than of their own. And what I was saying about goats was on this account: that all around where I live it is common, when country women run short of milk for their own children, to call goats in to help; and I have at this moment two men-servants who never sucked women's milk for more than eight days after they were born. These goats are quickly taught to come and nurse the little children, know their voices when they cry, and come running to them. If anyone else but the foster-child is presented to them, they refuse to let it suck, and the child likewise will refuse to suck another goat. I saw one the other day from which they had taken away the goat that used to nurse it, because the father had only borrowed it from a neighbour; the child would not touch any other they could bring, and died, no doubt of hunger. Beasts can change and corrupt their natural affection as easily as we do: I think there are many mistakes in what Herodotus relates about a certain region of Libya, where, he says, the women are held in common but the child, as soon as it can walk, picks his father out from the crowd, drawn to him first by natural inclination.

Now, considering this simple reason for loving our children — that we have begotten them, and so call them our second selves — it strikes me that there is another kind of offspring that comes from us no less deserving of recognition. For what we engender by the soul, the children of our understanding, of our courage, and of our abilities, springs from nobler parts than those of the body, and is much more our own; in this generation we are both father and mother. These cost us a great deal more and bring us more honour, if there is anything of good in them. As for our other children, their value is far more theirs than ours; the share we have in them is very little. But of these the whole beauty, all the grace and value, is ours, and they also represent us more vividly than the others. Plato adds that these are immortal children, who immortalise and deify their fathers, like Lycurgus, Solon, and Minos. Now, since history is full of examples of the common affection of fathers for their children, it does not seem inappropriate to bring in a few examples of this other kind. Heliodorus, that good bishop of Trikka, chose rather to lose the dignity, the income, and the devotion of so venerable a prelacy than to lose his daughter — a daughter who survives to this day, very graceful and shapely, but perhaps a little too carefully and wantonly dressed up, and too amorous for a clergyman's daughter. There was in Rome a certain Labienus, a man of great worth and authority and, among other qualities, excellent in every branch of literature, who was, I take it, the son of that great Labienus, the chief of Caesar's captains in the Gallic wars, who, afterwards taking Pompey's side, so valiantly held out his cause until he was beaten by Caesar in Spain. This Labienus I am now speaking of had several enemies, envious of his good qualities; and, very likely, the courtiers and favourites of the emperors of his time, who were highly offended at his independence and at the paternal spirit, hostile to tyranny, which he still kept up — with which we may suppose he had tinged his books and writings. His adversaries prosecuted several pieces he had published before the magistrates in Rome, and managed to have them condemned to the fire. It was on him that this new form of punishment was begun, which was later carried on against others at Rome: to punish writings and studies themselves with death. There would not be cruelty and material enough for cruelty, if we did not mix into it things that nature has exempted from all feeling and suffering, such as reputation and the products of the mind — if we did not extend bodily punishment to the teachings and monuments of the Muses. Now, Labienus could not endure this loss, nor outlive his so dear offspring, and so had himself conveyed and shut up alive in the tomb of his ancestors, where he managed to kill and bury himself at the same stroke. It is hard to show a more violent fatherly affection than this. Cassius Severus, a man of great eloquence and his very intimate friend, on seeing the books burned, cried out that by the same sentence they ought to condemn him to the fire as well, since he carried in his memory everything they contained. The same thing happened to Cremutius Cordus, who, being accused of having praised Brutus and Cassius in his books — that filthy, slavish, and corrupt Senate, worthy of a worse master than Tiberius, condemned his writings to the flames. He was willing to keep them company, and killed himself by starvation. The good Lucan, condemned by that scoundrel Nero, at the last gasp of his life, when most of his blood had already run out through the veins of his arms, which he had had his physician open to make him die, and when the cold had taken hold of his extremities and was creeping up towards his vitals, the last thing he had in his memory was some verses of his Pharsalia, which he recited, dying with them on his lips. What was this, but a tender and fatherly farewell to his children, in imitation of the goodbyes and embraces with which we part from ours when we come to die — and an effect of that natural inclination which suggests to our memory, in this last extremity, those things which were dearest to us during the time of our life?

Can we believe that Epicurus — who, as he says himself, dying of the unbearable pain of the stone, had all his consolation in the beauty of the doctrine he was leaving behind him — could have received the same satisfaction from many children, however well-conditioned and brought up, if he had had them, as he did from the production of so many rich writings? Or that, had it been his choice to leave behind him a deformed and dull child or a foolish and ridiculous book, he, or any other man of his understanding, would not rather have chosen to run the first misfortune than the other? It might, perhaps, have been an impiety in Saint Augustine, if, on the one hand, it had been proposed to him to bury his writings, from which religion has received such great fruit, or, on the other, to bury his children (had he had them), if he had not rather chosen to bury his children. And I do not know whether I would not much rather have begotten one perfectly beautiful book through association with the Muses than by lying with my wife. What I give to this, such as it is, I give absolutely and irrevocably, as men do to their bodily children. That little I have done for it is no longer at my own disposal; it may know things that have gone from me, and may hold from me what I have not kept; and which, as from a stranger, I should have to borrow back from it, if I needed it. If I am wiser than my book, it is richer than I. There are few men addicted to poetry who would not be much prouder to be the father of the Aeneid than of the handsomest youth in Rome, and who would not bear the loss of the one much better than the loss of the other. For according to Aristotle, the poet, of all artists, is the fondest of his work. It is hard to believe that Epaminondas, who boasted that, in lieu of any posterity, he was leaving behind two daughters who would one day do their father honour (meaning the two victories he won over the Spartans), would have willingly consented to exchange these for the most beautiful creatures in all Greece; or that Alexander or Caesar ever wished to be deprived of the greatness of their glorious deeds in war, for the convenience of children and heirs, however perfect and accomplished. Indeed, I greatly doubt whether Phidias, or any other excellent sculptor, would be as anxious about the preservation and continuance of his natural children as he would be about a rare statue, which he had brought to perfection by long labour and study according to his art. And as for those furious and disordered passions which have sometimes inflamed fathers towards their own daughters, or mothers towards their own sons, the like is also found in this other kind of parenthood: witness what is told of Pygmalion, who, having made the statue of a woman of singular beauty, fell so passionately in love with this work of his that the gods, in favour of his passion, breathed life into it.
"Tentatum mollescit ebur, positoque rigore, Subsidit digitis."
["The ivory grows soft under his touch and, its hardness gone, yields to his fingers." — Ovid, Metamorphoses, x. 283.]
